newsitem.title: UK: Dlr charges batteries in late Europe for new climb.
newsitem.headline: Dlr charges batteries in late Europe for new climb.

text.p: The dollar muscled to a new 34-month peak of 1.7210 marks in afternoon Europe, settling just below there in late trade as it charged its batteries for the next push high, analysts said.
Traders took heart from the fact dollar/mark stalled only briefly on news the rise in German jobless slowed last month.
"It all points to the underlying strength of the dollar," said Don Smith, international economist at HSBC Markets here.
New U.S. data came in firmer than expected, with weekly jobless claims falling to 310,000 from the previous week's 316,000. Economists had predicted a slight rise to 317,000.
U.S. January factory orders rose by 2.5 percent, outstripping the expected 2.0 percent increase and turning around a drop of 1.5 percent in December.
The dollar was trading at 1.7168/78 marks at 1626 GMT, up from late Wednesday's European level of 1.7110/15.
German seasonally-adjusted unemployment rose 5,000 to 4.316 million. The unadjusted total, however, was in line with the 4.672 million already leaked by German labour market sources.
After the jump in jobless seen in January, analysts said any kind of rise in February pointed up the underlying weakness in the German labour market.
The mark drew only slight support from news that January German manufacturing orders increased 2.4 percent on the month, a far bigger rise than the average 0.9 forecast.

"It's going to take a succession of strong numbers now for the the market to really start believing the German economy is picking up," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at Bank of America in London.

The market is now eagerly awaiting U.S. February non-farm payrolls figures, due at 1330 GMT on Friday. Expectations centre on a increase of 230,000 after growth of 271,000 in January. The jobless rate is seen edging down to 5.3 percent from 5.4.

Though a strong number is to some extent priced in, analysts said the current bullishness surrounding the dollar meant any downturn would be regarded as a buying opportunity, and any negative bond market reaction should have only a short-lived impact on the currency.
The hourly earnings rate and average workweek will be closely watched, with players ever watchful for pre-emptive Federal Reserve action against inflation.
"(Earnings data) remain the focus of market concern about interest rates -- the relationship between growth and inflation," said HSBC's Smith.
Dollar/yen was sidelined during most of the session and found its upside capped by mark/yen's slip to nine-month lows.

After spending much of the European afternoon drifting around 121.50 yen, the dollar tripped up in late dealings after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said a sustained Japanese current account surplus was "in nobody's interest".
The dollar stood at 121.10/20 yen at 1703 GMT, down from yesterday's close here of 121.34/29 and an intrasession high of 121.81.
Back in Europe, the Bundesbank surprised few by holding interest rates unchanged after its regular council meeting.
However, the Federation of German Trade Unions said the central bank should slash interest rates to stimulate economic growth if it was serious about fighting unemployment.
Meanwhile, the head of German industry association VDMA said a dollar/mark rate of 1.80-2.00 would be "more correct" than current levels.

Dollar/Swiss swept to a 38-month high of 1.4922 francs intraday, though had slipped back to 1.4845/52 by 1718 GMT. A similar story was true of sterling/mark, which hit a 53-month peak of 2.7733 before settling back at 2.7690/00 in late trade. -- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
